title: Walls Against Death: Reading Poe's 'The Masque of the Red Death'

source.title: The Masque of the Red Death

intro.summary: This source is a short story, not a research study, so its 'findings' are what happens in the plot and what readers take from it. A deadly plague called the Red Death sweeps the land. A rich prince, Prospero, locks himself and a thousand friends inside a walled abbey, welds the gates shut and throws a masked ball in seven coloured rooms. At midnight a guest dressed as a Red Death victim appears; the prince chases him, dies, and the guests find the costume is empty: the plague itself was inside all along, and everyone dies. The main limitation is that Poe never states a moral, so symbolic readings (for example, that the seven rooms stand for the stages of a life) are interpretations, and readers disagree about them. This lesson does not cover Gothic fiction as a genre, the history of the Black Death, Poe's own theories of the short story, or the long debate over whether the story is a strict allegory; these are good next topics.
background: A short story is a piece of fiction short enough to read in one sitting; this one is only a few pages long.
A plague is a disease that spreads quickly through a population and kills many people; real plagues such as the Black Death led some rich people to flee to isolated estates.
A masquerade is a party where guests wear masks and costumes, so no one can be sure who anyone really is.
A symbol is an object in a story that stands for a larger idea, the way a red rose often stands for love.
intro.aha: The prince's welded gates did not keep the Red Death out: the terrifying guest's costume was empty, because death itself had been inside the walls all along.

primer.heading: The question
primer.body: The story asks a question everyone faces sooner or later: can money, walls and fun keep death away? It opens with a terrible imaginary disease, the Red Death, which kills its victims within half an hour and marks their faces with blood. The story itself never states its question outright. It shows a man trying to answer it with a wall.
primer.quote: No pestilence had ever been so fatal, or so hideous.

primer.heading: What happens
primer.body: While half his country dies, Prince Prospero gathers a thousand healthy friends inside a fortified abbey. The courtiers weld the iron gates shut, so no one can get in or out. They decide that the suffering outside is not their problem. After five or six months they hold a grand masked ball in a strange suite of seven coloured rooms. The last room is black, has blood-red windows and holds a giant ebony clock that stops the party every hour.
primer.quote: With such precautions the courtiers might bid defiance to contagion. The external world could take care of itself.

primer.heading: What we find
primer.body: At midnight the guests notice a new masked figure dressed as a corpse spattered with blood: a costume of the Red Death. The furious prince chases him through all seven rooms and drops dead in the black room. When the guests seize the figure, they find nothing inside the mask and grave clothes. The disease itself had walked in, and every guest dies.
primer.quote: gasped in unutterable horror at finding the grave cerements and corpse-like mask, which they handled with so violent a rudeness, untenanted by any tangible form.

primer.heading: Why it matters, and its limits
primer.body: The ending turns every safety measure into a trap: the walls kept help out and the guests in, and death came anyway. Many readers see the story as being about mortality, the fact that everyone dies. On that reading, wealth and distraction can delay facing death but cannot escape it. Poe never spells this out, though. Readings such as 'the seven rooms are seven stages of life' are popular but are not stated in the text, so this lesson flags them as interpretations, not facts.
primer.quote: And Darkness and Decay and the Red Death held illimitable dominion over all.

concepts.title: The Red Death: a plague that kills fast and isolates its victims
concepts.idea: The Red Death is an imaginary plague that kills within half an hour and marks its victims with blood, which shuts them off from other people's help and sympathy.

terms.means: A deadly disease that spreads through a whole population, like a plague
Poe's phrase for the plague's visible mark: a sign that labels someone as infected and so pushes others away from them

concepts.recap: The Red Death kills in half an hour, and its bloody stains, especially on the face, mark victims so that others stop helping or pitying them.

understand.explanation: Edgar Allan Poe's short story opens by describing an invented plague called the Red Death. A pestilence is a deadly disease that sweeps through a whole population, and the story says no pestilence had ever been so fatal or so hideous. The symptoms come in a fixed sequence: sharp pains, sudden dizziness, heavy bleeding through the skin, and then death, all within half an hour. The worst part is social. Scarlet stains appear on the body and especially on the face, and Poe calls these marks the 'pest ban': a visible sign that cuts the sick person off from other people's help and sympathy. The story never ties the Red Death to any real disease. It is fiction, so read these details as the author's description, not as medical facts.
understand.quote: The scarlet stains upon the body and especially upon the face of the victim, were the pest ban which shut him out from the aid and from the sympathy of his fellow-men.

activities.prompt: Put an everyday illness beside the Red Death. Notice what other people do when they see each one.

cases.label: An ordinary bad flu (made-up example)
cases.text: You get a fever and stay in bed for a week. Nothing on your face tells strangers you are sick. Friends drop off soup, call to check on you, and feel sorry for you. The illness is slow enough for them to help, and nothing about how you look drives them away.

cases.label: The Red Death (from the story)
cases.text: Sharp pains, sudden dizziness, then 'profuse bleeding at the pores, with dissolution', all within half an hour. Scarlet stains cover the body and especially the face. The story says these stains were 'the pest ban which shut him out from the aid and from the sympathy of his fellow-men.'

activities.takeaway: In the made-up flu case, help keeps coming because the illness is slow and hidden. With the Red Death, the bloody marks are visible on the face, and the story says those marks shut the victim out from help and sympathy. The flu is only a contrast for illustration and is not in the story.

activities.question: According to the story, which detail is what shuts a Red Death victim off from other people's help and sympathy?

options.text: The scarlet stains on the body, and especially on the face
options.feedback: Right. The story names these stains as 'the pest ban which shut him out from the aid and from the sympathy of his fellow-men.' Because the mark is visible, especially on the face, everyone around can see who is sick and turns away.

options.text: The disease kills within half an hour
options.feedback: The speed is real and terrible: the story says the whole illness lasts 'half an hour.' But the story ties being cut off from help and sympathy to the visible stains, not to the timing.

options.text: The sharp pains and sudden dizziness
options.feedback: These are symptoms the victim feels inside, and the story does list them. Nobody else can see a pain or a dizzy spell, though. The story gives the job of shutting the victim out to the marks other people can see.

options.text: No earlier pestilence had ever been so fatal
options.feedback: The story does say this. It tells us how deadly the plague is, though, not why victims lose other people's help. The sentence about losing 'aid' and 'sympathy' is about the scarlet stains.

hints: Look for the sentence that uses the words 'aid' and 'sympathy'.
Which detail could other people see just by looking at the victim?

concepts.title: Prospero's plan: lock out the world
concepts.idea: Prospero tries to escape the plague by sealing his friends inside a walled abbey with welded gates, which keeps the world out but also locks everyone in.

terms.means: Shutting yourself away from other people, so that no one comes in or goes out
A large old building once used by monks or nuns; Prospero's is 'castellated', meaning built with castle-like walls
Old formal words for a way in (ingress) and a way out (egress)

concepts.recap: Prospero's walls and welded gates keep the plague's world out, but by removing every way out they also turn the abbey into a sealed trap for everyone inside.

understand.explanation: In the last concept you met the Red Death, a plague that kills in half an hour. When half of his lands have died, Prince Prospero does not try to help them. Instead he takes a thousand healthy, cheerful friends into an abbey, a big castle-like building, and shuts them away from the world; this shutting-away is called seclusion. The building already has a high wall and iron gates, but the courtiers go further and melt the gate bolts shut with furnaces and hammers. The old words ingress and egress mean a way in and a way out, and the story says the welding was meant to leave neither of them for anyone inside who might panic. Whether this plan protects them is a question the rest of the story answers; for now we only know the plan, and that its strongest lock faces inward as well as outward.
understand.quote: The courtiers, having entered, brought furnaces and massy hammers and welded the bolts. They resolved to leave means neither of ingress nor egress to the sudden impulses of despair or of frenzy from within.

activities.title: Prospero's precautions, one at a time, with the reason the story gives

steps.text: When does he act? Only 'when his dominions were half depopulated', that is, when half the people in his lands had already died.
steps.result: The plan starts late, and it is a plan to save himself and his circle, not his people.

steps.text: Who goes in? 'A thousand hale and light-hearted friends': people who are healthy (hale) and cheerful, taken from among the knights and ladies of his court.
steps.result: He picks guests who are well and in a good mood. No sick or poor people are let in.

steps.text: Where? 'The deep seclusion of one of his castellated abbeys', girdled by 'a strong and lofty wall' with 'gates of iron'.
steps.result: A wall and gates keep outsiders out, but gates can still be opened from the inside.

steps.text: The extra step: the courtiers 'brought furnaces and massy hammers and welded the bolts'. Welding melts the metal locks together so they can never be opened again.
steps.result: The stated reason points inward: no ingress and egress, no way in or out, 'to the sudden impulses of despair or of frenzy from within'. They fear their own panic too.

steps.text: Supplies: 'The abbey was amply provisioned.' There was plenty of food and drink stored inside.
steps.result: No one ever needs to leave, so a door is not needed for daily life.

steps.text: Pleasures and attitude: 'buffoons', 'musicians', 'ballet-dancers', 'wine', and the view that 'it was folly to grieve, or to think' and 'The external world could take care of itself.'
steps.result: The plan also seals out thought and grief. The guests are meant to forget what is happening beyond the wall.

steps.text: The story sums it up: 'All these and security were within. Without was the “Red Death”.' (Within means inside; without means outside.)
steps.result: The plan rests on one belief: danger is outside, safety is inside, and a wall can keep the two apart.

activities.takeaway: Each precaution has a stated purpose, but one of them, the welded bolts, works in both directions: it stops anyone coming in and also stops anyone getting out.

activities.question: Which precaution does the most to trap the guests inside as well as keep the world out?

options.text: Choosing a thousand healthy, light-hearted friends
options.feedback: This decides who comes in, but it puts no limit on leaving. It is about selecting guests, not locking doors.

options.text: The strong, lofty wall with gates of iron
options.feedback: Close, but not the strongest answer. A wall with gates still has gates, and gates can be opened from inside. It is the next step that takes that choice away.

options.text: Welding the bolts of the gates shut
options.feedback: Yes. Welding makes the gates impossible to open, and the story says the aim was to leave 'neither of ingress nor egress', no way in and no way out, for anyone inside who gave way to 'despair or of frenzy from within'. The lock faces both directions.

options.text: Stocking the abbey with plenty of food and drink
options.feedback: Supplies remove the need to leave, but they do not stop anyone who wants to. A full pantry is a comfort, not a lock.

options.text: Providing musicians, dancers, jesters and wine
options.feedback: The entertainment keeps people from thinking about the outside, which is a kind of mental wall. But it does not physically stop anyone from leaving; the welded bolts do.

hints: Ask of each option: does it stop someone who wants to leave?
Gates can be opened. What did the courtiers do to make sure they could not be?
Look for the step whose stated reason is about people 'from within'.

concepts.title: Seven rooms, east to west, ending in black
concepts.idea: The ball is held in seven winding rooms that run from a blue room in the east to a black room with blood-red windows in the west, and the guests avoid that last room.

predict.question: Picture a stage director who must pick one room in this layout for the night's most frightening moment. Using only what this part of the story describes, which room fits best?
options: The blue room, because the prince stands there
The orange room, because it sits in the middle and everyone passes through it
The black room, because its blood-red light and its emptiness already make guests afraid
Any room would do, because the colours are only decoration
why: The prince matters, but the blue room is the ordinary start of the line. Its glass matches its walls and it is full of dancers, so nothing about it signals dread.
A busy middle room seems like a good stage. But Poe puts the frightening room at the far western end, not in the crowd, and the middle rooms are where 'beat feverishly the heart of life'.
Right. It is the one room whose windows clash with its walls, its light makes faces look 'wild', and guests already refuse to go in. The setting has prepared the reader to fear it.
This is tempting if you read the rooms as scenery. But Poe chooses the colours with care: six rooms match and one breaks the pattern, and that break is what makes the guests stay away.

terms.means: A set of rooms joined one after another and used together, like a row of connected hotel rooms
A metal bowl or stand that holds burning coals or fire, used for light or heat

model.title: Map of the seven rooms, east to west
model.note: Teaching model: a bird's-eye plan with the seven rooms drawn as equal squares in a zigzag. Poe gives no sizes beyond 'a sharp turn at every twenty or thirty yards', so shapes and distances are illustrative, not from the story. The squares are not painted in the story's colours: each label names its room's colour. 'Crowded with dancers' is simplified to yes or no. Poe says that early on 'few' guests dared enter the black room, and that later in the night 'none' did.

controls.label: Which room you stand in (1 = east end)
Light the fires outside the windows

outputs.label: Turns west of the blue room
Windows match the walls (1 yes, 0 no)

steps.say: This is a map of seven rooms seen from above, joined in a zigzag. East is on the right, west on the left.
The dot is you. This slider walks you from room to room.
These boxes tell you whether your room's windows match its walls, and whether dancers crowd it.
This switch lights fires in a hidden passage outside the windows. They are the only light the rooms get, so watch the glow around you.
Back to the start. Let's walk through them.

explore.prompt: Walk the rooms yourself. Use what you just learned about the order of the colours and the one room the guests avoid.

goals.text: Stand in the last room that is still crowded with dancers before the room they refuse to enter
hints: Which room do the guests stay out of?
The crowded rooms run from the east end up to the room just before the one they avoid.
Walk west until the next step would make the crowd box drop to 0, and stop there.

goals.text: With the rooms lit, stand two rooms east of the room the guests are afraid to enter
hints: Two things are needed: light, and the right room.
No room has a lamp of its own, so the switch has to be on. Then find the feared room and count back toward the east.
East is toward the blue room, so from the black end you step back two rooms, not forward.

feedback.correct: Yes. Poe has already made the black room frightening before anything happens in it: its scarlet glass clashes with its black walls, its light makes faces look wild, and guests won't go in. A director would follow that design.
feedback.incorrect: You may have read the colours as scenery, or looked for the busiest room. But Poe builds a pattern (six rooms where glass matches walls) and then breaks it in the last, western room. That break, and the guests' refusal to enter, is what marks the black room as the place of fear.

steps.say: Start at the eastern end, in the blue room, with the fires lit. Poe calls this run of seven joined rooms a suite. Here the walls are blue, and so are the windows.
Where does the light come from? No lamp or candle burns in any room. Outside each window stands a brazier, a metal stand holding fire. Its light shines through the coloured glass.
Turn west into the purple room. The way bends sharply, so you see little more than one room at a time. Each turn brings a new surprise.
Green, then orange. In every room so far, the glass matches the walls.
White, then violet. All six of these rooms are packed with dancers.
Now the last, westernmost room. Black velvet covers the walls, ceiling and floor, but the windows are scarlet, a deep blood colour. It is the only room where glass and walls don't match.
Firelight through blood-red glass onto black cloth makes faces look ghastly. So the dancers stay out, and the crowd box drops to 0. The one room nobody enters lies at the very end of the line.

understand.explanation: The masked ball takes place in a suite of seven rooms laid out in a winding line. It runs from a blue room at the eastern end, through purple, green, orange, white and violet, to a black room at the western end. No room has a lamp. Each one is lit by a brazier outside its window, so each room glows the colour of its glass. In six rooms the glass matches the walls. In the black room alone the panes are blood-red, and the light they throw is so ghastly that few guests dare to go in. Poe doesn't tell us what this layout means. He describes it in careful detail, room by room, and readers have to decide for themselves why the frightening room sits at the far western end.
understand.quote: But in the western or black chamber the effect of the fire-light that streamed upon the dark hangings through the blood-tinted panes, was ghastly in the extreme, and produced so wild a look upon the countenances of those who entered, that there were few of the company bold enough to set foot within its precincts at all.
understand.quote_where: Description of the seven rooms, before the clock is introduced

connect.caption: The story has no equation. This is the model's own rule, written out. The blue 'room' term is the slider: rooms 1 to 6 have glass that matches their walls and are full of dancers. Room 7, the black room, breaks both patterns, and the match and crowded boxes drop to 0 there.

concepts.recap: Seven rooms run east to west from blue to black. Only the last room's blood-red windows clash with its walls, and the guests keep out of it.

activities.prompt: The rooms are scattered below, and some lines are doorways Poe never mentions. Trace the route a guest walks from the eastern end of the suite to the western end, in Poe's order.
hints: Start at the room Poe names first, at the eastern end.
The black room has to come last, and the room just before it is violet.
activities.explanation: Poe lists the rooms in order: blue at the eastern end, then purple, green, orange, white and violet, and finally black at the western end. The extra lines were shortcuts that don't exist. A guest has to pass through every room in turn, and the black room is always reached last.

concepts.title: The clock that interrupts the party
concepts.idea: Every hour the ebony clock's chime freezes the revel, the guests laugh it off and promise not to be shaken again, and the same unease returns at the next chime.

terms.means: A detail that comes back again and again in a story and gains meaning each time it returns, like a song's chorus

understand.explanation: A huge clock made of ebony, a dark wood, stands against the west wall of the black room, the one the guests avoid. Every hour its chime is so strange that the orchestra stops, the dancers freeze, the young guests go pale and the older ones rub their brows as if lost in thought. When the echoes fade, everyone laughs at their own nerves, and the musicians whisper promises that the next chime will not move them. Sixty minutes later the clock strikes again and the same unease returns, so the promise never holds. A detail that keeps coming back like this is called a motif, and each return adds weight to it. The story never says what the clock stands for. Many readers take it as a reminder that time, and life, is running out (a memento mori, an object that reminds us we will die), but that is a reading of the text, not something the text states.
understand.quote: the musicians looked at each other and smiled as if at their own nervousness and folly, and made whispering vows, each to the other, that the next chiming of the clock should produce in them no similar emotion; and then, after the lapse of sixty minutes, (which embrace three thousand and six hundred seconds of the Time that flies,) there came yet another chiming of the clock, and then were the same disconcert and tremulousness and meditation as before.
understand.quote_where: Fifth paragraph, the description of the ebony clock

activities.prompt: Put one hour of the party in order, from one chime of the ebony clock to the next.
items: The ebony clock strikes the hour with a loud, deep, strange note
The musicians pause and the waltzers stop dancing
The giddiest guests grow pale; older guests pass their hands over their brows
The echoes die away and light laughter spreads through the crowd
The musicians whisper vows that the next chime will not affect them
The clock chimes again and the same unease returns
hints: The guests can only laugh at their fear after the sound has stopped.
The promise about the next chime comes after the laughter, while they are smiling at their own nerves.
The last step mirrors the first: the cycle closes where it began.
activities.explanation: The story gives exactly this sequence: chime, music stops, faces go pale, echoes fade, laughter, vows, sixty minutes, chime again. The last step loops back to the first, so the cycle repeats all night. The vow sits just before the next chime, and that placement shows it failing: the very next chime brings back the 'same disconcert and tremulousness and meditation as before'.

activities.question: The guests keep trying to shrug off the chime, and keep failing. What do you think they are failing to ignore?

options.text: The passing of time: every hour that strikes is an hour of their lives gone
options.feedback: This reading has the strongest support in the passage. The narrator calls the hour 'three thousand and six hundred seconds of the Time that flies', with a capital T, and the guests react with 'confused reverie or meditation', not just surprise. The limit: the story never says this outright, so it remains an interpretation.

options.text: The plague raging outside the walls
options.feedback: There is some support. The ball takes place 'while the pestilence raged most furiously abroad', and the clock stands in the black room with blood-red windows, the colour of the Red Death. The limit: the clock passage itself never mentions the plague, so this link comes from the setting around the clock, not from what the chime is said to mean.

options.text: Just a loud noise that interrupts the music
options.feedback: The text does not support this. It describes the sound as 'clear and loud and deep and exceedingly musical', so it is not simply unpleasant, and the reactions go far beyond annoyance: the giddiest grow pale and the old fall into meditation. A mere noise would not explain why the same unease returns every hour.

options.text: Guilt about the people they abandoned outside
options.feedback: This is possible but thinly supported. The courtiers did shut out a dying country, and the story notes that 'the external world could take care of itself'. But guilt is never mentioned, and the reactions described, pallor and dazed reflection, fit fear or unease better than a troubled conscience.

concepts.recap: Each hour the clock forces the revellers to stop and feel uneasy; they laugh and vow to ignore it, but the feeling returns with every chime.

concepts.title: Midnight: the masked figure walks east to west
concepts.idea: At midnight a guest costumed as a Red Death victim walks unchallenged from the blue room through every room to the black one, and the prince who chases him dies there.

predict.question: Imagine a retelling where the masked figure walks the other way: from the black room east to the blue room, with the prince chasing behind. What would the walk lose compared with Poe's version?
options: The walk would no longer lead into the room the guests feared, with its clock and blood-red windows. The chase would end in the bright blue room instead.
Nothing. The direction of the walk carries no meaning.
The figure would pass through fewer rooms on the way.
The prince would have to get past the welded iron gates.
why: This fits the story. Poe's route heads for the black room the guests feared, with its clock and blood-red glass, and a reversed walk moves away from it. Poe never explains his choice, so this is a reading, not his statement.
Tempting if you treat the route as stage directions. But Poe names every room in order, and the walk ends in the one room the guests feared. Reversing it changes where the chase ends.
Someone might think direction changes distance. The suite is the same seven rooms either way, so a full walk still crosses all of them.
The gates are in the wall around the whole abbey, not in the suite. A walk from room to room never reaches them, in either direction.

terms.means: A fear and wonder so deep it has no name. Poe gives it as the reason nobody grabs the figure.
Someone in a mask and costume playing a part. This is Poe's word for the masked figure.

model.title: Map of the seven rooms, east to west: the midnight chase
model.note: Teaching model: a bird's-eye plan with the seven rooms drawn as equal squares in a zigzag. Poe gives no sizes beyond 'a sharp turn at every twenty or thirty yards', so shapes and distances are illustrative, not from the story. The squares are not painted in the story's colours; each label names its room's colour. The 'You' marker now stands for the masked figure: you walk in its footsteps. Poe gives the figure's route room by room and says the prince crossed 'the six chambers', but he gives no speeds or timings. Positions are therefore snapshots, not a timed chase. The rule 'the prince falls when both reach the black room' is the model's summary of the story's ending.

controls.label: Which room you stand in (1 = east end)
Light the fires outside the windows

outputs.label: Turns west of the blue room
Rooms the prince is behind the figure
Figure turns to face the prince (1 yes, 0 no)

steps.say: Same map as before: seven rooms, blue in the east, black in the west. The 'You' dot now walks in the footsteps of a masked stranger at the ball.
New: this slider moves Prince Prospero, the dot with his name. Watch him head west.
These boxes count how many rooms he trails behind, and whether he is still alive.

explore.prompt: Use the two sliders to rebuild the chase, one moment at a time, in the order Poe tells it.

goals.text: Recreate the moment just before the chase begins: the figure has walked as far as Poe says it got before anyone moved, and the prince is still where he gave his order.
hints: Think back to the walkthrough. Which room did Poe name last before 'a decided movement had been made'?
The prince hasn't moved yet, so leave his slider in the room where he shouted his order.
The figure has reached the room just before the dead end, but not the dead end itself.

goals.text: Bring the chase to its end: put the figure and the prince where the prince falls.
hints: Where does the figure stop walking and turn around?
The prince's dagger drops 'upon the sable carpet'. Which room has the black carpet?
Both dots must end up in the same room, at the far western end.

feedback.correct: Right. Poe's route always leads west, into the black room the guests avoided, with its clock and blood-red glass. Reverse it and the chase ends somewhere bright instead. This is a reading of the story: Poe never explains why he chose that direction.
feedback.incorrect: The route is not random stage direction. Poe names every room in order, from blue to violet, and the walk ends in the one room nobody dared enter. Reversing it would end the chase in the cheerful east.

steps.say: Midnight. As the clock's twelve strokes fade, the guests notice a stranger dressed as a Red Death victim, blood on his clothes and face. The prince, in the blue room, orders his courtiers to seize him.
The stranger walks right past him, within a yard. Nobody puts out a hand. Poe calls what grips them 'nameless awe': fear and wonder so deep it has no name.
On through purple, green, orange. The crowd shrinks back to the walls. The prince still hasn't moved, and the gap keeps growing.
Poe's word for the stranger is a mummer: someone in a mask and costume, playing a part. This one keeps the same slow, solemn step into the white room.

Only after the mummer has walked through the violet room does the prince, ashamed of his own fear, run after him with a drawn dagger. He runs alone: no courtier follows. Here he is mid-rush, as the figure enters the black room.
Light the fires. The blood-red glass glows. One room separates them now: the black room, with the ebony clock against its western wall.
When the prince steps in, the figure reaches the far wall, turns and faces him. A sharp cry, the dagger falls, and the prince drops dead on the black carpet. You'll stage that moment yourself next.

understand.explanation: At midnight the guests notice a stranger dressed as a victim of the Red Death. The prince orders him seized, but nobody touches him, because a 'nameless awe' holds everyone back. The figure walks slowly through the rooms in Poe's exact order, blue to purple to green to orange to white to violet, before anyone moves. Then the prince, ashamed, rushes alone through the six chambers. At the far end of the black room the figure turns, and the prince falls dead. This is a work of fiction, so the evidence is Poe's text itself: the map, the positions and the 'falls when both reach the black room' rule are our simplification, and Poe gives no timings.
understand.quote: he made his way uninterruptedly, but with the same solemn and measured step which had distinguished him from the first, through the blue chamber to the purple—through the purple to the green—through the green to the orange—through this again to the white—and even thence to the violet, ere a decided movement had been made to arrest him.
understand.quote_where: The paragraph after the prince's order in the blue room

connect.caption: Poe's story has no equation; this is the model's own rule. Blue is the figure's room (the 'room' slider), orange is the prince's room, and their difference is the gap box. When both reach room 7, the black room, the 'Prince is alive' box drops to 0.

activities.prompt: Trace the masked figure's walk at midnight, from where the prince gives his order to where the figure turns around. Watch out for routes the figure never took.
activities.explanation: Poe names every step: 'through the blue chamber to the purple—through the purple to the green—through the green to the orange—through this again to the white—and even thence to the violet', and the figure turns at 'the extremity of the velvet apartment'. The figure skips no room. The corridor lies behind the windows and holds the braziers, so it is not a route. The iron gates were welded shut and lie outside the suite.
hints: The figure walks slowly and takes no shortcuts.
The corridor is only seen through the windows, and the gates were welded shut.

activities.question: The prince shouts 'Seize him and unmask him!' and the figure passes within a yard of his courtiers. Why does no one grab him?

options.text: A 'nameless awe' inspired by the figure's costume holds them all back.
options.feedback: Supported. Poe writes that 'from a certain nameless awe with which the mad assumptions of the mummer had inspired the whole party, there were found none who put forth hand to seize him'.

options.text: They didn't hear the order over the music.
options.feedback: Not supported. The prince's words 'rang throughout the seven rooms loudly and clearly', and the music had stopped at the wave of his hand.

options.text: They thought the costume was a harmless joke and saw no reason to act.
options.feedback: Not supported. The guests felt 'terror, of horror, and of disgust', and Poe says the costume had gone beyond even the prince's loose rules of good taste.

options.text: The figure threatened them with a weapon.
options.feedback: Not in the text. The only weapon in the scene is the prince's own dagger. The figure simply walks with a 'solemn and measured step'.

hints: Look at what Poe says the party felt, not at anything the figure did.
Poe uses a two-word phrase for a fear too strong to name.

concepts.recap: Held back by nameless awe, nobody stops the masked figure as it walks every room from blue to black. The prince who finally chases it dies in the black room, where it turns to face him.

concepts.title: The empty costume: death was already inside
concepts.idea: The guests find nothing under the mask and grave clothes, because the figure is the Red Death itself given a human shape, so the walls that were meant to keep death out could never have worked.

terms.means: An old word for a person in costume at a masked party, like someone in a Halloween outfit
Grave clothes: the cloth wrapped around a dead body before burial
Empty, with nobody living inside, like a rented flat with no tenant
Showing a thing or idea, such as a disease, as if it were a person who can walk and act

concepts.recap: The welded gates kept people out, not death: the costume was empty because the Red Death had been inside the walls all along.

understand.explanation: When the revellers finally grab the mummer (the costumed stranger), they find his cerements, the grave clothes wrapped around a corpse, and his corpse-like mask untenanted: empty, with no body inside. The narrator then says the Red Death itself was present, so the figure is a personification, the plague shown as a person who walks and acts. This twist undoes Prospero's whole plan: welded gates and a high wall can stop people, but they cannot stop a disease, and they cannot stop death. The black room and the hourly clock had been reminders of death inside the abbey the whole time, and the guests had laughed them off. Poe never explains how the plague got in, so reading the ending as a lesson that no wealth or wall can shut death out is an interpretation it invites, not something the narrator states outright.
understand.quote: seizing the mummer, whose tall figure stood erect and motionless within the shadow of the ebony clock, gasped in unutterable horror at finding the grave cerements and corpse-like mask, which they handled with so violent a rudeness, untenanted by any tangible form.
understand.quote_where: Final paragraphs, just after Prospero dies

activities.question: At midnight a guest dressed as a victim of the Red Death walks through all seven rooms. The prince chases him into the black room and drops dead when the figure turns to face him. Before you read on, who do you guess is under the mask?

options.text: One of the thousand guests, playing a cruel joke
options.feedback: A sensible first guess. Masked balls are full of jokes, and the prince himself assumes this when he asks who dares to insult him. Keep it in mind and see whether the ending agrees.

options.text: Someone from outside who got past the wall
options.feedback: Reasonable if you think the walls had a weak spot. But remember that the gates were welded shut. Watch for whether the story ever shows anyone breaking in.

options.text: No one: the costume is the plague itself
options.feedback: A bold guess. It would mean the figure is not a person at all. See whether the evidence in the next screens backs this up.

options.text: I can't tell yet
options.feedback: Fair enough. The story keeps the answer back until the very end. Let's look at the evidence in the order Poe gives it.

activities.prompt: Here is how the ending unfolds, one step at a time. Watch what the guests find and what it means for Prospero's walls.

stages.label: 1. The prince falls
stages.text: Prospero runs after the figure with a dagger. In the black room the figure turns, there is a sharp cry, and the prince falls dead on the black carpet. The guests now find the courage of despair and rush into the room they had all been avoiding.

stages.label: 2. They seize the stranger
stages.text: The figure stands still in the shadow of the ebony clock. Poe calls him the mummer, an old word for a person in costume at a masked party. The guests grab him roughly, expecting to unmask a man.

stages.label: 3. The costume is empty
stages.text: Under the hands of the guests are only the cerements (grave clothes, the cloth wrapped around a corpse) and the corpse-like mask. Poe says they were untenanted by any tangible form: empty, with no body inside, like a flat with no tenant. Nobody was ever wearing the costume.

stages.label: 4. Death is named
stages.text: The narrator says: "And now was acknowledged the presence of the Red Death. He had come like a thief in the night." The figure was the plague shown as a person. This is called personification: a thing or idea, here a disease, drawn as someone who walks and acts. The phrase "like a thief in the night" echoes a well-known Bible line and means arriving unseen and unannounced.

stages.label: 5. Everything stops
stages.text: One by one the revellers drop dead in the halls. The ebony clock stops when the last of them dies, and the fires in the tripods go out. Darkness, Decay and the Red Death rule over everything.

stages.label: 6. Look back at the walls
stages.text: The courtiers had welded the iron gates so that nobody could get in or out. No gate was opened, and yet death was in the room. The black chamber and the chiming clock, both part of Prospero's own design, had been reminding the guests of death inside the walls from the start.

activities.takeaway: The prince's welded gates did not keep the Red Death out: the terrifying guest's costume was empty, because death itself had been inside the walls all along.

activities.question: Which passage tells you that the Red Death got in without anyone opening the gates?

options.quote: And now was acknowledged the presence of the Red Death. He had come like a thief in the night.
options.feedback: Correct. A thief in the night arrives unseen. The plague is present, but nobody saw it come in, so the locks were never tested and never mattered.

options.quote: The courtiers, having entered, brought furnaces and massy hammers and welded the bolts.
options.feedback: This describes the precaution, not how it failed. It is what makes the ending a shock: the gates were truly sealed.

options.quote: With such precautions the courtiers might bid defiance to contagion.
options.feedback: This is the courtiers' belief that the walls would protect them. The ending shows that belief was wrong, but this line does not show death arriving.

options.quote: The external world could take care of itself.
options.feedback: This shows the guests' attitude toward everyone left outside. It says nothing about how death came in.

hints: Look for a line that describes an arrival, not a plan.
Which line names the Red Death as being present?

activities.title: Walls against death
activities.prompt: Sort each item. Was it a precaution meant to keep death away, or a sign that death was already inside the abbey?

groups.label: Precaution meant to keep death away (it failed)
Sign that death was already inside

cards.text: Iron gates with the bolts welded shut
cards.feedback: A precaution. It stopped anyone from walking in, yet the Red Death was in the black room all the same.

cards.text: A strong, high wall around the abbey
cards.feedback: A precaution. A wall stops people and animals. It cannot stop the thing it was built against.

cards.text: Plenty of food stored, so no one had to go out
cards.feedback: A precaution. It kept the guests from meeting the outside world, but death did not need anyone to go out and fetch it.

cards.text: Inviting only a thousand healthy, cheerful friends
cards.feedback: A precaution. The story calls them hale, meaning healthy. Choosing well people did not keep the plague away in the end.

cards.text: The rule that it was foolish to grieve or think
cards.feedback: A precaution of the mind: if you never think about death, perhaps it cannot touch you. The clock kept forcing that thought back, and in the end the rule failed too.

cards.text: The ebony clock whose hourly chime froze the party
cards.feedback: A sign. The clock stood in the black room and reminded everyone, every hour, that time and life were running out. It stops when the last guest dies.

cards.text: The black room with blood-red windows that guests avoided
cards.feedback: A sign. Prospero built it himself. Its blood-coloured panes echo the Red Death's scarlet marks, and it is where the prince dies.

cards.text: Grave clothes and a mask with no body inside
cards.feedback: A sign, and the clearest one. The empty costume shows the figure was the plague itself, not a guest who slipped in.

activities.takeaway: Every precaution was built to stop people. The signs of death were built into the party itself, so the walls were guarding against the wrong thing.

activities.question: Go back to your first guess. What was really under the mask, and what does that mean for Prospero's walls?

options.text: Nothing: the Red Death itself had taken a human shape, so walls built to stop people could never stop it
options.feedback: Correct. The guests find the grave clothes untenanted, and the narrator then acknowledges the presence of the Red Death. A wall is no barrier to something that is not a person.

options.text: A guest playing a cruel joke, who died of fright
options.feedback: That is what the prince assumed, but the story rules it out. When the guests seize the figure, the costume is empty, with no body inside.

options.text: An outsider who climbed the wall
options.feedback: The story never shows anyone breaking in, and the gates stayed welded. Also, an outsider would have had a body; the costume had none.

options.text: A wearer who slipped out of the costume before the guests grabbed it
options.feedback: The text does not support this. The figure stood erect and motionless by the clock until it was seized, and then the narrator names it as the Red Death.

hints: What did the guests feel when they grabbed the costume?
Reread stage 3: what does untenanted mean?

activities.question: Poe never says exactly how the Red Death got inside. Which reading do you find most convincing? There is no single right answer here.

options.text: It slipped in unseen: "like a thief in the night" means it simply arrived, and locks don't matter to a plague
options.feedback: Well supported by the narrator's own words about arrival. The limit: the story never shows a moment of entry, so 'slipping in' is filled in by the reader.

options.text: It was inside all along: the black room and the clock show death was built into the abbey from the start
options.feedback: Supported by how Prospero designed the rooms and by the clock that stops when the last guest dies. The limit: these are symbols, so the reading depends on treating the rooms and clock as meaningful, which the narrator never says outright.

options.text: It is a lesson: no one, however rich or well protected, can shut out death
options.feedback: This is the reading the ending most clearly invites, in the spirit of a memento mori (a reminder that you will die). The limit: Poe never states a moral, so this is an interpretation of the story, not a claim it makes.

options.text: It is a literal supernatural event and needs no deeper meaning
options.feedback: The story does present it as real within its world: the guests truly die. The limit: this reading has trouble explaining why Poe gives so much detail to the coloured rooms and the clock.
